# Where Caliper differs from react-docgen-typescript and the checker

Caliper aims for correct types for Storybook and for agents. TypeScript's checker is the arbiter of a prop's type. Agreement with react-docgen-typescript (RDT) is information, not a goal. Where Caliper differs from RDT only because RDT is wrong or less precise, that is intended. Where Caliper is not better, it is a gap, and this page says so.

RDT is a fair reference for a reason that also limits it: it prints the checker's own type text, alias names kept. On most props RDT and the checker are the same string, so "Caliper differs from RDT" almost always means "Caliper differs from the checker", and the question is whether that is acceptable. Caliper is better than RDT in one class only (RDT truncates or picks the wrong declaration). Everywhere else the honest label is "acceptable difference" or "gap".

Each class below has four parts: what differs, why we think Caliper is better (or "not better: a gap" and the fix direction), how the weekly record measures it (and whether the comparator scored it right), and how it is accounted for. The examples were run with Caliper built from `main` at `c5fbb33e` with the weekly record's flags (`--html-attributes full --include-unexported --load-dependencies --collapse-inherited-props none`), RDT from `apps/oracle` with the options of `scripts/rdt.mjs`, and TypeScript 6.0.3 from `apps/oracle` for the checker text. The verdicts are `apps/oracle/src/oracle.ts` run on the same file (the oracle's own checker is `7.1.0-beta`). Caliper's output is the canonical JSON type with empty `description` fields dropped.

## How the numbers are produced

`scripts/weekly.py --oracle` extracts each pinned corpus with the flags above, then `apps/oracle/src/oracle.ts` asks TypeScript 7.1's checker for the type of every own prop of every exported function whose only parameter, or `props` parameter, is the props type. Own means not declared by `@types/react`, and not `ref` or `key`. A prop both sides list is **shared**, and gets one verdict from the structural comparison in `apps/oracle/src/oracle-compare.ts`:

- **identical**: the same type.
- **spelled**: the same type, Caliper naming what the checker expands (or the reverse).
- **less precise**: Caliper's type is looser, unevaluated, or spelled in a way the comparator has not seen.
- **wrong**: Caliper's type describes something else.
- **checker any/error**: the checker has no type (unresolved import, `any`).

`agree` is identical plus spelled over the shared props. It is the looser number: `less precise` hides real imprecision and, as the classes below show, some real errors. `wrong` is the number that matters, and the gate: the weekly issue opens above 0.1% of the judged props (`docs/measurement.md`, "The headline"). `wrong` both over-triggers (a comparator artifact, classes 1 to 3) and under-triggers (silent wrong answers scored `less precise`, class 5), so read it with this page.

Measured 2026-11-06 on `main` at `c5fbb33e`, the pinned corpora, `scripts/weekly.py --oracle`:

| Corpus   | Shared props | Less precise | Wrong | Checker any/error |  agree |   wrong | RDT wrong (same props) |
| -------- | -----------: | -----------: | ----: | ----------------: | -----: | ------: | ---------------------: |
| mantine  |       20,104 |        1,828 |     0 |                 8 |  90.9% |       0 |                  0.04% |
| chakra   |      486,832 |           22 |     1 |                 0 | 100.0% | 0.0002% |                 0.006% |
| shadcn   |       13,863 |          738 |     8 |                60 |  94.2% |  0.058% |                  0.59% |
| antd     |        3,426 |          205 |     0 |                 1 |  94.0% |       0 |                  1.05% |
| spectrum |        2,023 |          100 |    22 |               208 |  83.7% |   1.09% |                  5.02% |

The last column is `oracle.tools.rdt.wrong_listed`: the share of the props RDT lists that the checker contradicts. react-docgen throws on 51 of 295 antd files and 265 of 1,240 shadcn files (17% and 21%) and so omits their props.

The 31 wrong verdicts are 28 index-signature artifacts (class 1), 2 silent call-signature errors (class 4) and 1 narrower type from a factory (class 6). The 3,201 shared props that are not agree are 2,893 less precise, 31 wrong and 277 checker any/error.

## Classes

### 1. Index signatures (comparator artifact, fixed in the comparator fix)

**What differs.**

```ts
type Layout = { [id: string]: number }
props: { layout?: Layout; slots?: { [slot: string]: boolean } }
```

- RDT: `layout` is `Layout`, `slots` is `{ [slot: string]: boolean; }`.
- Caliper: `{"kind":"object","fields":[{"name":"id","propType":{"kind":"number"},"required":true,"indexKey":{"kind":"string"}}]}` for `layout`, and the same shape with `slot` for `slots`.
- Checker: `Layout | undefined` and `{ [slot: string]: boolean; }`.
- Verdict on main: `wrong` for both props.

**Why.** Caliper is right: the canonical JSON states an index signature as a field carrying `indexKey`, and the type is the one the checker prints. The comparator reads that field as a property named `id` or `slot`, which the checker's type does not have.

**Measured.** 28 of the 31 `wrong` are this, and all 28 are false. After the comparator fix an index signature is compared as an index signature and these props are identical or spelled. Until it merges, spectrum's 22 wrong (1.09%) are above the gate for this reason alone.

**Accounted.** Documented here; the comparator fix removes it.

### 2. `readonly` (comparator artifact, fixed in the comparator fix)

**What differs.**

```ts
props: { tuple?: readonly [number, string] }
```

- RDT: `readonly [number, string]`.
- Caliper: `{"kind":"readonly","element":{"kind":"tuple","elements":[{"type":{"kind":"number"}},{"type":{"kind":"string"}}]}}` (schema version 5 wraps each element to carry its marker and label).
- Checker: `readonly [number, string] | undefined`.
- Verdict on main: `less precise`.

**Why.** Same type, so Caliper is right. The comparator does not know the `readonly` kind and reads it as unevaluated.

**Measured.** 22 props across the corpora score `less precise` for this. After the fix the comparator looks through `readonly`.

**Accounted.** Documented here; the comparator fix removes it. It moves `less precise` into `identical`, so it moves `agree` and not `wrong`.

### 3. `'a' | string` against `string & {}` (comparator artifact, fixed in the comparator fix)

**What differs.**

```ts
type Size = 'sm' | 'md'
props: { size?: Size | (string & {}) }
```

- RDT: `Size | (string & {})`.
- Caliper: `{"kind":"union","members":[{"kind":"stringLiteral","value":"sm"},{"kind":"stringLiteral","value":"md"},{"kind":"string"}]}`.
- Checker: `Size | (string & {}) | undefined`.
- Verdict on main: `less precise`.

**Why.** Caliper writes the pattern's meaning: the literals, then any string. It does not keep the `& {}` trick that stops an editor collapsing the union. For Storybook that is the right control (a select of the literals plus free text) and the type accepts the same values. The comparator scores a `string` beside literals as widening.

**Measured.** About 166 props score `less precise` for this. After the fix the comparator reads `string` beside the checker's `string & {}` as the same type.

**Accounted.** Documented here; the comparator fix removes it.

### 4. Call-signature-only types become an empty object

**What differs.**

```ts
type Fn = { (x: number): string }
type Watch<T> = { (): T; (name: keyof T): T[keyof T] }
props: { f?: Fn; w?: Watch<{ x: number }> }
```

- RDT: `Fn`, `Watch<{ x: number; }>`.
- Caliper: `{"kind":"object","fields":[]}` for both.
- Checker: `Fn | undefined`, `Watch<{ x: number; }> | undefined`.
- Verdict: `wrong` for both. The component has no diagnostics and the props have no `degradedBy`.

Measured 2026-11-06 on `main` at `c5fbb33e`, the pinned corpora, `scripts/weekly.py --oracle`:

| Corpus   | Shared props | Less precise | Wrong | Checker any/error |  agree |   wrong | RDT wrong (same props) |
| -------- | -----------: | -----------: | ----: | ----------------: | -----: | ------: | ---------------------: |
| mantine  |       20,104 |        1,828 |     0 |                 8 |  90.9% |       0 |                  0.04% |
| chakra   |      486,832 |           22 |     1 |                 0 | 100.0% | 0.0002% |                 0.006% |
| shadcn   |       13,863 |          738 |     8 |                60 |  94.2% |  0.058% |                  0.59% |
| antd     |        3,426 |          205 |     0 |                 1 |  94.0% |       0 |                  1.05% |
| spectrum |        2,023 |          100 |    22 |               208 |  83.7% |   1.09% |                  5.02% |

The last column is `oracle.tools.rdt.wrong_listed`: the share of the props RDT lists that the checker contradicts. react-docgen throws on 51 of 295 antd files and 265 of 1,240 shadcn files (17% and 21%) and so omits their props.

The 31 wrong verdicts are 28 index-signature artifacts (class 1), 2 silent call-signature errors (class 4) and 1 narrower type from a factory (class 6). The 3,201 shared props that are not agree are 2,893 less precise, 31 wrong and 277 checker any/error.

## Classes

### 1. Index signatures (comparator artifact, fixed in the comparator fix)

**What differs.**

```ts
type Layout = { [id: string]: number }
props: { layout?: Layout; slots?: { [slot: string]: boolean } }
```

- RDT: `layout` is `Layout`, `slots` is `{ [slot: string]: boolean; }`.
- Caliper: `{"kind":"object","fields":[{"name":"id","propType":{"kind":"number"},"required":true,"indexKey":{"kind":"string"}}]}` for `layout`, and the same shape with `slot` for `slots`.
- Checker: `Layout | undefined` and `{ [slot: string]: boolean; }`.
- Verdict on main: `wrong` for both props.

**Why.** Caliper is right: the canonical JSON states an index signature as a field carrying `indexKey`, and the type is the one the checker prints. The comparator reads that field as a property named `id` or `slot`, which the checker's type does not have.

**Measured.** 28 of the 31 `wrong` are this, and all 28 are false. After the comparator fix an index signature is compared as an index signature and these props are identical or spelled. Until it merges, spectrum's 22 wrong (1.09%) are above the gate for this reason alone.

**Accounted.** Documented here; the comparator fix removes it.

### 2. `readonly` (comparator artifact, fixed in the comparator fix)

**What differs.**

```ts
props: { tuple?: readonly [number, string] }
```

- RDT: `readonly [number, string]`.
- Caliper: `{"kind":"readonly","element":{"kind":"tuple","elements":[{"type":{"kind":"number"}},{"type":{"kind":"string"}}]}}` (schema version 5 wraps each element to carry its marker and label).
- Checker: `readonly [number, string] | undefined`.
- Verdict on main: `less precise`.

**Why.** Same type, so Caliper is right. The comparator does not know the `readonly` kind and reads it as unevaluated.

**Measured.** 22 props across the corpora score `less precise` for this. After the fix the comparator looks through `readonly`.

**Accounted.** Documented here; the comparator fix removes it. It moves `less precise` into `identical`, so it moves `agree` and not `wrong`.

### 3. `'a' | string` against `string & {}` (comparator artifact, fixed in the comparator fix)

**What differs.**

```ts
type Size = 'sm' | 'md'
props: { size?: Size | (string & {}) }
```

- RDT: `Size | (string & {})`.
- Caliper: `{"kind":"union","members":[{"kind":"stringLiteral","value":"sm"},{"kind":"stringLiteral","value":"md"},{"kind":"string"}]}`.
- Checker: `Size | (string & {}) | undefined`.
- Verdict on main: `less precise`.

**Why.** Caliper writes the pattern's meaning: the literals, then any string. It does not keep the `& {}` trick that stops an editor collapsing the union. For Storybook that is the right control (a select of the literals plus free text) and the type accepts the same values. The comparator scores a `string` beside literals as widening.

**Measured.** About 166 props score `less precise` for this. After the fix the comparator reads `string` beside the checker's `string & {}` as the same type.

**Accounted.** Documented here; the comparator fix removes it.

### 4. Call-signature-only types become an empty object

**What differs.**

```ts
type Fn = { (x: number): string }
type Watch<T> = { (): T; (name: keyof T): T[keyof T] }
props: { f?: Fn; w?: Watch<{ x: number }> }
```

- RDT: `Fn`, `Watch<{ x: number; }>`.
- Caliper: `{"kind":"object","fields":[]}` for both.
- Checker: `Fn | undefined`, `Watch<{ x: number; }> | undefined`.
- Verdict: `wrong` for both. The component has no diagnostics and the props have no `degradedBy`.

  • Components: the same name in the same source file. We show how many components with RDT props Caliper also found.
  • Props found: RDT’s non-React props present on those shared components. This is recall against RDT, not proof that every type is correct.
  • Same control: for props both report, the type maps to the same Storybook control kind: boolean, number, text, select, function, node or object.
  • Same text: exact type text after RDT’s own normalization. “Same or cosmetic” also forgives formatting differences such as union order and Array<T> spelling.
type resolution

Unbound generics

A conditional or mapped type can stay opaque when its type parameter has no concrete value. Nested inference can leave part of a type unresolved.

component discovery

Anonymous wrappers

Some wrapper calls without a type argument and some styled-component forms are still missed by the default extractor.

The experimental TypeScript 7.1 checker can recover some harder types on exported function components. It is opt-in and was off for this 0.4.0 run.

RDT can miss or widen types too. Caliper sometimes keeps literal choices that RDT prints as string. That is why we also ask TypeScript 7.1’s checker to compare the structure of a prop type: literals, unions, object fields, function parameters and index signatures.

The checker run labels shared props as identical, differently spelled, less precise or wrong. On the October baseline, shadcn/ui has 14.5% “less precise” and 0.1% “wrong” against that oracle; Spectrum has 30.2% “less precise,” mostly a responsive type printed without its object form. These are separate results with a different component set from the RDT chart above.

The checker used for this measurement is separate from Caliper’s experimental TypeScript-backed extraction pass.

Ant Design has no committed lockfile, so its dependencies are freshly resolved. The harness logs any other install that needs a fresh resolve. These are Caliper 0.4.0 results from October 23; newer extraction work needs a rerun. The measurement page shows the timing boundaries.

Two props are wrong with no warning: a type made only of call signatures comes back as an empty object. They are the ones we most want fixed. The experimental TypeScript 7.1 checker can recover some harder types on exported function components. It is opt-in and was off for these runs.

TypeScript’s checker does. It knows the type of every prop, so we ask it for each one and compare both tools with it by the same rules. RDT is not the reference. It prints the checker’s own type text, so it agrees on most props, and where it does not, it is sometimes the one that is wrong.

RDT’s list also holds entries that are not components: hooks, helpers and context providers, and one component repeated under every file that re-exports it. On Ant Design it lists 258 entries. With those taken out, 202 remain, and Caliper reports 186 of them (92.1%, November 2). A bar of “props found against RDT” would count the rest against Caliper, which is why it is not the headline here.

The comparison has known flaws that count some right answers as wrong. The differences page lists each class with an example and says whether the comparison scored it right.

Ant Design has no committed lockfile, so its dependencies are freshly resolved. The harness logs any other install that needs a fresh resolve. RDT and react-docgen run once each. The measurement page shows the timing boundaries.

content.text:
The parity page now opens with the checker's verdicts instead of recall against RDT, using the 2026-11-06 weekly record. I screenshotted the full page at desktop width in light theme only. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0, and I didn't run the site build or `verify`.

**Your question.** The narrative is right on correctness and not proven on completeness. On the share of listed props the checker contradicts, Caliper is lower on all five libraries. The recall bars made Caliper look worse mainly because RDT's list includes non-components and repeats. On Ant Design, RDT lists 258 entries and 202 remain once those are removed. "Fewer props, better result" isn't safe as a general claim, though. When an omitted prop counts against a tool, the two are about even: 44.7% against 44.8% on Ant Design, and 90.4% against 84.8% on shadcn/ui. The page says that outright.

**What the page now shows:**
- **Lead:** a one-scale bar chart of the wrong share per library. The figures are Caliper 0 to 1.09% and RDT 0.006 to 5.02%. A line under the chart says Caliper's numbers are upper bounds, because 28 of its 31 wrong verdicts are the comparison misreading index signatures.
- **Short read:** the correctness figure beside the "about even" completeness figure.
- **Scorecard:** the counts behind the bars (props compared, agrees, less precise, wrong).
- **Rest of the page:**
  - Verdict definitions.
  - The gaps, now including the two silent-wrong call-signature cases.
  - A "Who decides what is right?" section, with the checker as arbiter and why recall against RDT isn't the headline.
  - The method.
- **Code:** `ComparisonBars` gained an opt-in `scale="shared"` prop. The measurement page still uses the default.
- **Main page:** the "Go deeper" card now says "Are the props right?" with `0–1.09%`.

Open items:
- **Unused component:** `ParityPlot` is now unused. I haven't deleted it.
- **Unmeasured fix:** these numbers predate the comparison fix. A fresh weekly run would shrink Caliper's wrong share, but that costs money and is your call.
- **Unsourced figure:** the "0.38 s cold" card on the measurement page is still unsourced.
- **Nothing committed.** The pages-repo changes are uncommitted.

27:**Why not better: a gap, and a wrong one.** The same utility written inline in the prop keeps its name and arguments. Reached through an alias, `resolve_type_alias_type` (`crates/core/src/resolver/alias.rs`) forwards `Partial`, `Required`, `Omit` and `Pick` to the base type, so an omitted key reappears, a picked-out key set is the whole base, and a `Partial` loses its optionality. Fix direction: make the alias path return what the inline path already returns (the utility as a `named` type with the base as its argument), or evaluate the key set and the modifier. In Mantine this is the `classNames` and `styles` props of about 230 components, 487 occurrences.
29:**Measured.** Scored wrongly. The comparator compares an object's field names and not whether a field is optional, so a `Partial` or `Required` that lost its modifier scores `identical`, and Mantine's `Partial<Record<…>>` scores `less precise`. Only a changed key set reaches `wrong`, as `viaAlias` and `picked` do above. In the weekly record the Mantine occurrences are in `less precise`, never in `wrong`, so the gate does not see them.

The cases where the checker evaluates (`Parameters`, `ReturnType`) are not better: Caliper does not evaluate those two utility types, and RDT shows the value. content.content:
### 8. Caliper is more complete than RDT

**What differs.**

```ts
props: { big?: { field0: number; …80 fields… } | null; many?: …60 object variants… }
```

- RDT: `{ field0: number; field1: string; … 66 more ...; field79: string; } | null` and `{ kind: "variant0"; value0: number; } | … | { ...; } | ... 54 more ...`.
- Caliper: the 80 fields and the 60 variants in full (checked: a union of an 80-field object and `null`, and a union of 60 objects).
- Checker (printed without truncation): the full text.
- Verdict: `identical` for both.

**Why Caliper is better.** RDT prints the checker's type text with its default truncation, so a long type reaches Storybook as `… 54 more ...`, which is not a type. Caliper keeps all of it. The weekly dump also has two cases of RDT picking the wrong declaration (Chakra's `AccordionItem.value` is `string[]` in RDT, `string` in the checker and Caliper) and an incomplete enum (Chakra's `ColorPickerChannelInput.channel`); I did not re-run those here.

**Measured.** RDT's truncated text is unreadable to the oracle's adapter, which scores it `less precise` and never `wrong` (`apps/oracle/src/tool-norm.ts`), so RDT's wrong rate in the table is, if anything, low.

**Accounted.** Nothing to account for in Caliper. The RDT side is the last column of the table above.

### 9. Opaque, with a marker

**What differs.**

```ts
type E = { a: string; b: number }
props: { v?: React.ComponentProps<'input'>['value']; e?: E[keyof E]; tab?: 0 | -1 }
```
----CLASS8
### 8. Caliper is more complete than RDT

**What differs.**

```ts
props: { big?: { field0: number; …80 fields… } | null; many?: …60 object variants… }
```

- RDT: `{ field0: number; field1: string; … 66 more ...; field79: string; } | null` and `{ kind: "variant0"; value0: number; } | … | { ...; } | ... 54 more ...`.
- Caliper: the 80 fields and the 60 variants in full (checked: a union of an 80-field object and `null`, and a union of 60 objects).
- Checker (printed without truncation): the full text.
- Verdict: `identical` for both.

**Why Caliper is better.** RDT prints the checker's type text with its default truncation, so a long type reaches Storybook as `… 54 more ...`, which is not a type. Caliper keeps all of it. The weekly dump also has two cases of RDT picking the wrong declaration (Chakra's `AccordionItem.value` is `string[]` in RDT, `string` in the checker and Caliper) and an incomplete enum (Chakra's `ColorPickerChannelInput.channel`); I did not re-run those here.

**Measured.** RDT's truncated text is unreadable to the oracle's adapter, which scores it `less precise` and never `wrong` (`apps/oracle/src/tool-norm.ts`), so RDT's wrong rate in the table is, if anything, low.

**Accounted.** Nothing to account for in Caliper. The RDT side is the last column of the table above.

### 9. Opaque, with a marker
----CLASS16
### 16. RDT's own quirks

What RDT does that Caliper does not, run on small files:

- It drops `children` when the props type is an inline object literal. `function Kids2(props: { children?: React.ReactNode; label?: string })` lists only `label` in RDT; with the same members in a named interface RDT lists `children`. Caliper lists `children` in both, and the checker has it.
- It prints a generic inconsistently: `string | null` for one prop and `Value[]` for the next (class 12).
- It truncates long types (class 8).
- It reports any function with an object-like parameter as a component. For `export function helper(label: string)` RDT lists 50 props, `String`'s methods (`charAt`, `concat`, …), and Caliper reports no component.
- It lists `ref` and `key`, and one component per re-export (`docs/measurement.md`, "The reference").
- It omits whole components: in the weekly record the props of components RDT does not report are 403 (shadcn), 5,957 (chakra), 3,662 (antd) and 2,699 (spectrum) (`missing_by_reason.component`).

**Why Caliper is better.** Each of these is RDT being wrong or incomplete, so it is intended that Caliper differs.

**Measured.** RDT's score against the checker is in the table (`oracle.tools.rdt`), by the same rules as Caliper's. The reference for recall removes the non-components and the repeats (`docs/measurement.md`).

**Accounted.** The reference rules are documented; a recall figure against RDT is information.

### 17. Collapsed inheritance layers

**What differs.** With the default `collapseInheritedProps: dependencies`, a dependency source past the size rule becomes a layer of names. For a props interface extending a 35-prop `SpaceStyleProps` from a package:

- RDT lists `gap3` as `string | number`.
- Caliper, default collapse: 1 prop listed, and `gap3` is a name in the layer's `members` (35 of them), with no type. With `none`: 36 props listed and `gap3` has its type.
- Checker: `gap3 : string | number | undefined`.

  • Right and present: the tool lists the prop and its type is the checker’s, or the same type spelled differently, such as by name where the checker expands it. A prop the tool leaves out counts against it.
  • Less precise: the tool’s type is looser or left unevaluated. It does not contradict the checker.
  • Wrong: the tool’s type describes something else. This is the number we gate on.
  • Not counted: the checker has no type either, as with an unresolved import.

A conditional or mapped type can stay opaque when its type parameter has no concrete value. Nested inference can leave part of a type unresolved.

component discovery

Some wrapper calls without a type argument and some styled-component forms are still missed by the default extractor.

TypeScript’s checker does. It knows the type of every prop, so we ask it for each one and compare both tools with it by the same rules. RDT is not the reference. It prints the checker’s own type text, so it agrees on most props, and where it does not, it is sometimes the one that is wrong.

RDT’s list also holds entries that are not components: hooks, helpers and context providers, and one component repeated under every file that re-exports it. On Ant Design it lists 258 entries. With those taken out, 202 remain, and Caliper reports 186 of them (92.1%, November 2). These show the kind of mistake. The weekly record keeps counts and does not yet list the props behind them, so we cannot point from a count to every prop. A truncated type is scored less precise, never wrong, so it is in the counts above only as less precise.

  • Right and present: the tool lists the prop and its type is the checker’s, or the same type spelled differently, such as by name where the checker expands it. A prop the tool leaves out counts against it.
  • Less precise: the tool’s type is looser or left unevaluated. It does not contradict the checker.
  • Wrong: the tool’s type describes something else. This is the number we gate on.
  • Not counted: the checker has no type either, as with an unresolved import.
type resolution

Unbound generics

A conditional or mapped type can stay opaque when its type parameter has no concrete value. Nested inference can leave part of a type unresolved.

component discovery

Anonymous wrappers

Some wrapper calls without a type argument and some styled-component forms are still missed by the default extractor.

A zero is not a clean bill. The comparison scores a lost Partial or Omit as less precise, not wrong; in Mantine that touches about 230 components’ classNames and styles. The experimental TypeScript 7.1 checker can recover some harder types on exported function components. It is opt-in and was off for these runs.

TypeScript’s checker does. It knows the type of every prop, so we ask it for each one and compare both tools with it by the same rules. RDT is not the reference. It prints the checker’s own type text, so it agrees on most props, and where it does not, it is sometimes the one that is wrong.

RDT’s list also holds entries that are not components: hooks, helpers and context providers, and one component repeated under every file that re-exports it. On Ant Design it lists 258 entries. With those taken out, 202 remain, and Caliper reports 186 of them (92.1%, November 2). A bar of “props found against RDT” would count the rest against Caliper, which is why it is not the headline here.

The comparison has known flaws in both directions, and the differences page lists each class with an example and whether the comparison scored it right.

Ant Design has no committed lockfile, so its dependencies are freshly resolved. The harness logs any other install that needs a fresh resolve. RDT and react-docgen run once each. The measurement page shows the timing boundaries.

content.text:
The parity page now uses the November 9 weekly record (Caliper 0.10.0). It states counts with their denominators, groups the results into better, close and behind, and includes examples of what "wrong" means. I screenshotted it at desktop width in light theme only. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0, and I did not run the site build or `verify`.

On your percentage question: the 1.09% and 5.02% were weakly framed. The November 9 record has real counts, and Caliper's wrong count has since dropped. Caliper has 2 props the checker contradicts across the five libraries. RDT has 289 (138 on React Spectrum, 76 on shadcn/ui). The page now shows those counts, and each chart group says how many props RDT lists. On 0.04%: it was never meaningful, since it is 9 props on Mantine. I removed the percentages and the "5×/10×/30×" labels. Those ratios rested on one or eight props, and the 1.09% was entirely the comparison's own flaw.

- **Better:** wrong types (2 against 289). On Chakra, RDT leaves 16,642 props looser than the checker's type, and Caliper leaves 19.
- **Close:** of the props each tool lists, the two are level on Ant Design (94.2% against 93.8%). Caliper leads on Chakra and shadcn/ui, and RDT leads on Mantine and React Spectrum.
- **Behind:** completeness, where a prop left out counts against a tool. RDT is ahead on Mantine, Chakra and Spectrum. On Spectrum, Caliper reports 454 of 1,085 components and RDT reports 536. The page says so outright.
- **Examples:** four kinds of RDT mistake, each labelled "real library" or "small file". They come from the differences doc: a wrong declaration on Chakra's `AccordionItem.value` (`string[]` against `string`), a truncated 80-field type, `children` dropped, and a helper function treated as a component.
- **Caveats:** the page notes that RDT's count is a floor, because truncated types score "less precise" and never "wrong". A zero for Caliper is not a clean bill: a lost `Partial` or `Omit` scores "less precise".

**The gap that matters for trust:** the weekly record keeps counts but not the props behind them. The examples show the kind of mistake, not the actual 289, and the page says that. To close it, the weekly job should write the first 15 wrong props per library into `weekly.json`. That is a Caliper-repo change and I haven't planned a trail for it. Say if you want one.

Open items:
- **Unused component:** `ParityPlot` is now unused. I haven't deleted it.
- **Unsourced figure:** the "0.38 s cold" card is still on the measurement page, unsourced.
- **Stale one-sidedness:** the parity page cites the Ant Design "202 remain, 186 reported" figure from the November 2 pairing, not November 9.
- **Nothing committed.** The pages-repo changes are uncommitted.

You were right: the old three-bullet read mixed measures, so Mantine and Spectrum showed up under both "Close" and "Behind". It's now one verdict per library, each stated per measure. I screenshotted the new section at desktop width in light theme only. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0, and I did not run the site build or `verify`.

It follows one rule: "close" means within two points, and wrong types are counts rather than shares. Here is what each library shows, against the November 9 record:

| Library | Wrong types | Props both list | Completeness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| shadcn/ui | better (0 against 76) | better (94.5% against 88.1%) | better (90.8% against 84.8%) |
| Ant Design | better (1 against 36) | close (94.2% against 93.8%) | close (44.9% against 44.8%) |
| Chakra | better (1 against 30) | better (100.0% against 96.8%) | behind (92.3% against 95.7%) |
| React Spectrum | better (0 against 138) | close (84.7% against 86.3%) | behind (30.7% against 42.5%) |
| Mantine | better (0 against 9) | behind (93.6% against 97.1%) | behind (91.9% against 95.4%) |

The section lede now carries the summary: "Caliper is rarely wrong and sometimes less complete."

- **Mantine** is the weakest library for Caliper. It leaves 1,281 props "less precise" against RDT's 576.
- **Ant Design's** low completeness is stated as a shared limitation, not a win. Each tool leaves out about 3,700 props of components it doesn't report.
- **Caveat:** the wrong-type win is the strongest claim and rests on the checker's judgement. The page notes that RDT's count is a floor and that Caliper's zero isn't a clean bill.

message.content:
From the agent working on caliper:



<pasted_content id="7572">
The numbers match the Nov 9 record exactly, but the label "Completeness" misleads, and the page shouldn't present it as how complete Caliper is. I downloaded the Nov 9 weekly.json (artifact of run 42637254796, kept in ~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/weekly-2026-11-09/) and checked.

What the number measures: "agree over the universe". The universe is every own prop the checker finds on any exported function whose only parameter is a props type. That includes functions that aren't components. docs/measurement.md says to read it as a comparison between tools, "not as a share of real components".

Ant Design (44.9% vs 44.8%): a universe artifact, not incompleteness.
- The universe is 7,199 props. Both tools omit about 3,700 of them, almost all for the reason "component": neither tool reports that function as a component.
- For the 185 components Caliper does report, it found all 185 and misses 0 props. Its agreement over those is 94.2%, with 1 wrong.
- So "low completeness is a shared limitation" is accurate, but "44.9% complete" invites the reading that Caliper finds under half of antd's props, which is false.

React Spectrum (30.7% vs 42.5%): a real gap, 11.8 points.
- The universe is 5,582 props. Caliper lists 2,023 and RDT lists 2,747.
- The stratum breakdown of what's missing:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬───────┐
│ Where the checker declares the missing props │ Caliper │  RDT  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ Dependency                                   │ 741     │ 14    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ The component's own file                     │ 637     │ 702   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ Another project file                         │ 2,089   │ 2,098 │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴───────┘

- Almost the whole difference is props declared in dependencies. 741 of 5,582 is 13%, which covers the 11.8 points.
- For the 454 components Caliper reports, it misses 20 props and gets 0 wrong. Its agreement over those is 83.8%. That's weaker than antd, because 208 props have no checker type.
- I haven't established why Caliper skips those 741 props. The record has counts, not per-component lists. It could be components whose props come from dependency types not being detected, or something in how Spectrum re-exports. I can find out with scripts/reference_sample.py or scripts/layer_only_props.py, which need the Spectrum corpus. That's a corpus fetch, so I'd want your go.

Corrections for the page
- Rename "Completeness" to something like "Agreement over every prop the checker finds", and say next to it that it includes non-components.
- Add the figures that answer "what does Caliper miss in what it reports": antd 0 missing and Spectrum 20 missing props.
- Keep Spectrum "behind" as a stated limitation, with the dependency-declared props named as the likely cause. Don't call it a shared limitation.
- Your other cells look consistent with the record. The "0 against 138" Spectrum figure is RDT's 5.02% of 2,747 listed, which gives 138. I didn't check the Mantine, Chakra and shadcn figures. One caution: the Spectrum 0 wrong is new. The 2026-11-06 record had 22, which the comparator fix cleared, so the page should date its sources.
</pasted_content id="7572">

type resolution

Unbound generics

A conditional or mapped type can stay opaque when its type parameter has no concrete value. Nested inference can leave part of a type unresolved.

109
component discovery

Anonymous wrappers

Some wrapper calls without a type argument and some styled-component forms are still missed by the default extractor.

110
111

A zero is not a clean bill. The comparison scores a lost Partial or Omit as less precise, not wrong; in Mantine that touches about 230 components’ classNames and styles. The experimental TypeScript 7.1 checker can recover some harder types on exported function components. It is opt-in and was off for these runs.

112
113 114 115 116
117

TypeScript’s checker does. It knows the type of every prop, so we ask it for each one and compare both tools with it by the same rules. RDT is not the reference. It prints the checker’s own type text, so it agrees on most props, and where it does not, it is sometimes the one that is wrong.

118

RDT’s list also holds entries that are not components: hooks, helpers and context providers, and one component repeated under every file that re-exports it. On Ant Design it lists 258 entries. With those taken out, 202 remain, and Caliper reports 186 of them (92.1%, November 2). A bar of “props found against RDT” would count the rest against Caliper, which is why it is not the headline here.

119

The comparison has known flaws in both directions, and the differences page lists each class with an example and whether the comparison scored it right.

lines: <PageSection id="meaning-heading" label="definitions" title="What do the verdicts mean?" content="text">

-
  • Right and present: the tool lists the prop and its type is the checker’s, or the same type spelled differently, such as by name where the checker expands it. A prop the tool leaves out counts against it.

+
  • Agrees, all props: the tool lists the prop and its type is the checker’s, or the same type spelled differently, such as by name where the checker expands it, over every prop the checker finds. A prop the tool leaves out counts against it, and the checker’s functions include some that are not components.
• Less precise: the tool’s type is looser or left unevaluated. It does not contradict the checker.
• Wrong: the tool’s type describes something else. This is the number we gate on.
• Not counted: the checker has no type either, as with an unresolved import.

lines: <PageSection id="meaning-heading" label="definitions" title="What do the verdicts mean?" content="text">

-
  • Agrees, all props: the tool lists the prop and its type is the checker’s, or the same type spelled differently, such as by name where the checker expands it, over every prop the checker finds. A prop the tool leaves out counts against it, and the checker’s functions include some that are not components.

+
  • Agrees: of the props a tool lists, the share whose type is the checker’s, or the same type spelled differently, such as by name where the checker expands it.
• Less precise: the tool’s type is looser or left unevaluated. It does not contradict the checker.
• Wrong: the tool’s type describes something else. This is the number we gate on.
• Not counted: the checker has no type either, as with an unresolved import.

lines: <PageSection id="oracle-heading" label="the arbiter" title="Who decides what is right?" content="text">

TypeScript’s checker does. It knows the type of every prop, so we ask it for each one and compare both tools with it by the same rules. RDT is not the reference. It prints the checker’s own type text, so it agrees on most props, and where it does not, it is sometimes the one that is wrong.

-

RDT’s list also holds entries that are not components: hooks, helpers and context providers, and one component repeated under every file that re-exports it. On Ant Design it lists 258 entries. With those taken out, 202 remain, and Caliper reports 186 of them (92.1%, November 2). A bar of “props found against RDT” would count the rest against Caliper, which is why it is not the headline here.

+

With those taken out, 202 remain, and Caliper reports 188 of them (93.1%). A count of every prop RDT lists would charge Caliper for the rest, which is why it is not the headline here.
The comparison has known flaws in both directions, and the differences page lists each class with an example and whether the comparison scored it right.

- **Tables:** two small tables replace the old ones. One has agreement, wrong and less-precise counts for both tools. The other has Caliper's component coverage and own-props coverage, 99.3–100% of RDT's own props on those components. A note says what "real components" means and that RDT is the source of that list, so it isn't scored on it.

content.text:
No, not here. The `{ orin dx }` kicker is the brand's endorsement line, which the brand guide lists as one of the two uses of curly braces: section labels and that endorsement. It earns its place where a tool appears away from orin-dx.com, such as a social card or the tool's own repo. On the site it only repeats what the nav and the breadcrumb already say.

- **Other openers:** they use the same kicker row for something meaningful: "the idea" on Principles, "the family" on Tools, "the evidence" on my abandoned sub-page attempt. `ToolHero` hard-codes the text, so the tool pages can't.
- **Third repeat:** the row sits under `tools / build / caliper` and above a `build` chip. The family appears three times, and "orin dx" a fourth time in the nav.
- **Empty space:** I'd keep the row's space when there's nothing to say, as you suggest. The opener anatomy fixes the kicker's position and size so every page's title sits at the same height. Dropping the row would shift the title up on tool pages only.

What I'd do: give `ToolHero` a `kicker` prop (text, or empty with the same height) and default tool pages to empty on this site. The endorsement text could come back for off-site contexts. Sub-pages could carry a real label such as "the evidence" or "the method". The one decision for you is whether a tool page should ever carry text there. The candidate is the tool's job (for Caliper, "build with better inputs"), but that repeats the breadcrumb and the chip. I lean towards empty.

I haven't changed anything. Say yes and I'll add the prop, make the default empty, and give the evidence pages a real label.

result: The `{ orin dx }` kicker is the brand endorsement and repeats nav and breadcrumb on this site, so I recommend a `kicker` prop on `ToolHero` that defaults to empty with the same height. No change made, pending your yes.

content.content:
| `size` | `sm`, `md`, `lg`. One control scale (height, inline padding, text style) shared by every control. A test asserts that every component with `size` has the same height at each step; two named exceptions: SegmentedControl `sm`, which is the 24px nav toggle cell (`size.toggle.cell`) and meets the 24px target floor, not the 44px coarse-pointer target; and text inputs and Select (SPEC-008) use the `body` text style at every size, so their text never falls below `text.inputMin` (iOS Safari zooms a focused field under 16px). |
| `variant` | Visual emphasis within a component: `primary`, `secondary`, `ghost`. |
| `tone` | Semantic colour: `neutral`, `accent`, `danger`, `success`. Domain colour (an Orin tool `family`) maps to a tone. |
| `type` | Not a design prop. It stays the native attribute on buttons and inputs. |
| state | `disabled`, `pending`, `invalid`, `readOnly`, `required`, plus `pressed` or `selected` where the pattern needs one. Plain boolean names; wrappers translate React Aria's `isDisabled`. |
| values | `value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange(value)`. A single choice is a scalar and a multiple choice is an array, whatever the primitive returns. A control with no value yet takes `null` and renders its pending frame. Exceptions: Select's `null` means nothing is selected and the placeholder shows (its options are data, so its server HTML is never pending), and Menu's radio group `null` means no item is checked; RadioGroup uses `''` for none selected. |
| open state | `open`, `defaultOpen`, `onOpenChange(open)`. |
| position | `placement`, `offset`, `collisionPadding`, defaulting from tokens. |
| composition | `render` (element or `(props, state)`), `classes`, `ref` as a prop. No free `style` or `className`. |

### Markup

- The root carries `data-recipe`, `data-slot` and the design props as `data-size`, `data-variant`, `data-tone`.
- State is exposed only as our own attributes: `data-state` (`open | closed | on | off`, plus `mixed` on Checkbox), `data-orientation`, `data-disabled`, `data-pending`, `data-motion` (transition status: on overlays absent at rest, `starting` on enter and `ending` on exit; on SegmentedControl `ready` once the first paint has settled, so a known value never animates in), `data-current`, `data-highlighted` (Menu items and Select options, set by our wrapper). Design-time choices CSS needs are `data-placement`, `data-fill` and `data-modal` on overlays and `data-grouped` (`horizontal | vertical`) on a Button, Link or Toggle inside an attached group. Recipes style only these and ARIA attributes, never a library's own attributes, so swapping or upgrading a primitive never touches CSS.
- Parts are named by role: `Root`, `Trigger`, `Content`, `Item`, `Indicator`. We expose one anatomy of our own, not the primitive's (Base UI's `Positioner` and `Popup` are one `Content` to us).
- A control renders a pending frame of its own size while its state is unknown, and the real control the moment it has the state. It never renders a guess.

### Behaviour

Every default the primitive leaves open gets one decision, recorded in a table and tested: tab activation, whether a menu closes on selecting a check or radio item, hover delay, dismissal, focus return, Escape. The table is filled in per component when it is specified.

## Rules

Agreed 11 Oct:

1. Composition over configuration.
2. CSS before logic.
3. Mobile first; container queries over breakpoints. Media queries only for user preferences (motion, contrast, color scheme, hover, pointer, print, forced colors, scripting).
4. Semantic tokens at the design-system layer; components consume only semantic tokens.
5. `sva` and `cva` with semantic props, not `css()` and not inline style.
6. Never `!important`. Avoid inline style; it may carry a data-driven custom property (a swatch colour) and nothing else.

Adopted with them:

content.text:
Neither alone: the kicker text is a prop, and the system's rule ("composition over configuration", agreed 11 Oct) says my earlier `art` and `meta` props should have been composition.

**The kicker: a text prop, named `label`.** The sibling openers already do this: `Hero` and `PageIntro` both take `label: string` for the same row ("the idea", "the family"). `ToolHero` is the outlier because it hard-codes "orin dx". Text is content, so a prop fits, and the sibling name keeps the three openers consistent. When `label` is omitted the row keeps its height and renders nothing, so the title doesn't move.

**What I got wrong earlier.** The `art: 'mark' | 'strands' | 'none'` enum and the `meta: boolean` I added to `ToolHero` are exactly the configuration flags rule 1 argues against.
- `ToolHero` already has `mark`, `stage` and `actions` as `ReactNode` slots, which is the composition shape.
- `art` should be the caller passing what it wants into the art slot: the mark, `<LitLattice/>` plus `<Ribbon/>`, or nothing. `PageIntro` already works this way with `art?: ReactNode`.
- `meta` should be `stage` made optional, with the chip row rendering only when something is passed.
- The lattice's family colour (and the haze only when there's a mark) would live in the component as a default, not in a flag.

So I'd refactor those two props into slots, add `label`, and make the default empty. It's a small change, but it modifies the API I added earlier in this session, so it's your call. The family-tinted lattice in every mode still works. The tests I wrote would change shape to check what the caller passes.

Say yes and I'll do it in that order: slots first, then `label`, then the evidence pages passing their own label.

content.text:
It didn't flow, so I restructured it. The page now reads as one argument: the checker first, then three evidence sections, then the Mantine causes. I screenshotted the full page at desktop width in light theme only. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0, and I did not run the site build or `verify`.

What was wrong and what changed:
- **Judge too late:** the checker's role came after five sections that relied on it. "Who decides what is right?" is now first, with a closing line that sets up the three questions.
- **Table interrupting the story:** the counts table sat between the coverage chart and the examples that explain RDT's 289. The examples now follow the wrong-count chart, and the counts table closes the evidence.
- **Examples added a consequence column:** each shows what a reader of the docs would see, such as "the wrong control for the prop" or "text that is not a type".
- **Falls-short cards replaced:** the generic cards are now Mantine's actual causes, from the record. Of its 40 unreported components, 26 are compound members such as `Combobox.Dropdown`, 6 are sub-components in files with others, 4 are helpers that aren't components and 4 are factory-built. Its 1,281 less-precise props come from aliases left unexpanded, with counts from the November 6 doc.
- **Redundant text trimmed:** I folded the Ant Design "258 entries, 202 remain" line into the coverage chart's note.

Where other pages still need work:
- **Measurement page:** it's still all October, 0.4.0, and it is the next page with this problem.
  - The "0.38 s cold" card and the cold-run chart are unsourced.
  - The "28× RDT median" and the request-time figures predate the lazy session and 0.10.0.
  - It has no narrative thread, no "how much better" detail (your earlier ask), and no per-library speed. I'd restructure it the same way: claim, how measured, evidence, limits.
- **Main Caliper page:**
  - The "Why Caliper" intro still opens with a generic claim.
  - The workflow evidence line is the October 24 number.
  - The 28× card is October 0.4.0.
  - The "Types in. Controls out." and "What those types look like" sections predate the checker story.
  - The roadmap and features still need the audit fixes: add "how it works", add a comparison, and show a real TOON sample.
- **Shared hero:** the kicker and the `art`/`meta` composition refactor are still waiting on your yes.
- **Dead code:** `ParityPlot` is unused and still in the repo.

The caveat that matters for trust is unchanged: the examples show kinds of mistake, not the actual 289, because the weekly record has counts and no per-prop rows. Fixing that is a Caliper-repo change.

Nothing in the pages repo is committed. Which page next: the measurement page, the main page, or the hero refactor?

content.text:
Both fixes are in. The pairs in the counts table now scan at a glance, and the examples use the existing `TypeBoundaries` list instead of my local cards. I checked both at desktop width in light theme only. The `orin` and `orin-dx` gates (format, typecheck, lint, test) all exit 0, and I did not run the site build or `verify`.

**Pairs:**
- **Row colour:** each Caliper row is brass and its RDT row is muted. These are the same focus and reference colours the three charts use, so the table and the bars read as one system.
- **Group rule:** a heavier rule (2px against the hairline) closes each Caliper/RDT pair, and the last row still has none.
- **Library names:** the second row's name is muted too, so the bold names run down the column once per pair.
- **Table API:** I added two optional props to the existing `Table`: `groupSize` and `rowTones`. Both are plain data, and the recipe styles them through `data-*` attributes, per the rules. I added tests that cover marked groups, row tones and a table without either. I used props because `.astro` pages can't pass styled spans into a React component, and a new wrapper component was the thing you didn't want.

**Examples:** your critique was right on both counts: they were local cards in a 2×2 grid. They are now `TypeBoundaries` items stacked full width, with a highlighted code block per example and the declaration, RDT's output and the checker's in one block each. I deleted the five local style constants.

- **Code blocks:** they show line numbers, because that's `TypeBoundaries`' default. For three-line snippets that is noisy, and I can turn them off for this use.
- **Rule weight:** the 2px rule is subtle on screen. A darker colour for the group rule would help, if the tokens have a suitable border colour. I haven't tried it.

Nothing is committed in the pages repo.

content.text:
No, not for RDT, and the page should say so. Here is what the record does and doesn't scope, and I'll fix the table's description.

- **Caliper's columns** (wrong, agrees, less precise): scored over the props of components Caliper reports. Caliper doesn't report helper functions as components, so they're out by construction. The record's `caliper` and `caliper_reported` figures are identical.
- **RDT's columns:** scored over every prop RDT lists in the checker's universe: any exported function whose parameter is a props type. RDT reports hooks, helpers and context providers as components. For React Spectrum, 291 of RDT's 1,319 entries were excluded as non-components, so some of its 138 wrong and 52 less-precise props may belong to things that aren't components. Mantine, Chakra, shadcn/ui and Ant Design have far fewer excluded entries (21, 73, 21, 43), but the same caveat applies.
- **Real components:** this column is the only one restricted to real components, via the cleaned reference list.

So the table compares Caliper-on-components against RDT-on-everything-it-lists. If anything that flatters Caliper's wrong count and inflates RDT's. I can't size the effect, because the record has no per-prop rows. The proper fix lives in the Caliper repo: score RDT on the cleaned component set too, and publish that as its own field. Until then the page should state the limit beside the table.

Every figure in the counts table matches the November 9 record exactly, so nothing is miscounted. The count of props across components is a misleading unit, though, and the shares tell a different story. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0. I looked at the table render before the final wording edits and didn't re-screenshot after.

**What the table was hiding**
- A "less precise" count of Chakra RDT 16,642 against Caliper 19 looked like a landslide. It is 3.2% against 0.004% of listed props, and Chakra's props are heavily repeated across components.
- On the share, Caliper is worse than RDT on three of five libraries: Mantine 6.4% against 2.9%, React Spectrum 5.0% against 1.9%, and Ant Design 5.7% against 5.2%. It is better only on shadcn/ui (5.0% against 10.9%) and Chakra.
- Every "wrong" and "less precise" cell now shows the count and its share of the props that tool lists, for example `9 (0.04%)` and `1,281 (6.4%)`. The description now states the unit: a prop on 700 components counts 700 times.
- The "Where Caliper falls short" description now names Spectrum as well as Mantine. We know Mantine's causes, but not Spectrum's, so the section says "here is what we know".
- The description paragraph is shorter than before.

**What I couldn't resolve: the agent's earlier caveat.** I read "wasn't so right" as the pasted note about the "completeness" label, which I already fixed. If the agent said something else about the counts that I haven't seen, paste it and I'll check it against the page. The record has no per-prop rows, so these things remain open:
- how much of RDT's wrong and less-precise counts comes from functions that aren't components;
- how many distinct causes sit behind the repeated props.

Both need the Caliper-side change I described, so the counts can be restricted to real components and deduplicated.

Nothing is committed in the pages repo.

content.content:
The shared harness costs about 0.32 s, so the measured gap inside extraction is larger than the end-to-end bars suggest. The 0.38 s result is not an isolated Rust timer.

This corpus is copied fixtures with no installed package tree. It is good for the three-tool comparison, but it cannot tell us how Caliper handles types from a real project’s dependencies.

Seven runs per library on an Apple Silicon laptop; Caliper’s shown time is its best wall time. The 28× headline is the median of five library ratios. Caliper’s clock includes process start and JSON output; RDT’s parse time excludes Node startup.

Chakra is the memory outlier: 1,461 MiB with dependencies loaded. The speedup alone would hide that cost.

For parity, each repo is pinned to a commit and installed with its own package manager. We remove tests, stories, demos and declaration files, then give both tools the same source files. Caliper uses full HTML attributes, includes unexported components and loads installed dependencies.

We match components by file and name. On shared components we count RDT’s non-React props that Caliper finds; on shared props we compare Storybook control kinds and type text. A separate TypeScript 7.1 checker run tests type structure because RDT is not ground truth. Explore the prop results.

The weekly parity run checks these rates against a committed baseline and flags growing loss patterns. When comparing a new build with a base build, the harness interleaves their runs and flags a slowdown over 10% on any library. The baseline’s old timing is a record, not the speed gate.
1

Save a file

The component source changes while Storybook stays open.

2

Check freshness

The session checks saved edits before answering a docgen request.

3

Resolve the story

The on-demand path asks for the component the story needs.

4

Return prop docs

Storybook gets argTypes, defaults and descriptions.

On-demand resolution shipped in the 0.10.0 addon. These source results predate it and are not package benchmarks.

The biggest win came from replacing a JavaScript directory sweep on every request with one native freshness check per story. Session startup also stopped sending every component’s props to JavaScript just to build an index.

These times cover the addon’s request path. They do not include browser rendering, Storybook’s UI work or a full page load. The before and after builds ran interleaved, best of three.
  • Version matters. The five-library parity numbers are Caliper 0.4.0 from October 23. Newer releases need the same run again.
  • The clocks differ. Cold Node startup is shared; installed-library Caliper time includes process start while RDT time does not; addon request time leaves out browser rendering.
  • Project shape matters. A large dependency graph can raise both latency and memory. The pinned repos expose that cost better than fixture files alone.
  • TypeScript 7.1 is separate. The checker is a measurement oracle. Caliper’s semantic extraction pass is an experimental CLI opt-in in source, not a Storybook feature yet.
  • Prop parity across five libraries
  • Back to Caliper

The weekly parity run checks these rates against a committed baseline and flags growing loss patterns. When comparing a new build with a base build, the harness interleaves their runs and flags a slowdown over 10% on any library. The baseline’s old timing is a record, not the speed gate.
1

Save a file

The component source changes while Storybook stays open.

2

Check freshness

The session checks saved edits before answering a docgen request.

3

Resolve the story

The on-demand path asks for the component the story needs.

4

Return prop docs

Storybook gets argTypes, defaults and descriptions.

On-demand resolution shipped in the 0.10.0 addon. These source results predate it and are not package benchmarks.

The biggest win came from replacing a JavaScript directory sweep on every request with one native freshness check per story. Session startup also stopped sending every component’s props to JavaScript just to build an index.

These times cover the addon’s request path. They do not include browser rendering, Storybook’s UI work or a full page load. The before and after builds ran interleaved, best of three.
  • Version matters. The five-library parity numbers are Caliper 0.4.0 from October 23. Newer releases need the same run again.
  • The clocks differ. Cold Node startup is shared; installed-library Caliper time includes process start while RDT time does not; addon request time leaves out browser rendering.
  • Project shape matters. A large dependency graph can raise both latency and memory. The pinned repos expose that cost better than fixture files alone.
  • TypeScript 7.1 is separate. The checker is a measurement oracle. Caliper’s semantic extraction pass is an experimental CLI opt-in in source, not a Storybook feature yet.

content.text:
The measurement page has the same problems the parity page had, and more. The main page is mostly fixed, with a few leftovers. Both pages should draw on the same November 9 weekly record the parity page now uses. I haven't changed either page yet.

**Measurement page**
- **Stale and wrong:**
  - Everything is October on Caliper 0.4.0, and the "0.38 s cold" figure and its chart are unsourced.
  - It says "the weekly parity run checks against a committed baseline". That's false: the baseline workflows were removed, and the previous run is the baseline.
  - "The checker is not a Storybook feature yet" is also out of date. The on-demand addon shipped in 0.10.0.
- **Current data is available.** The November 9 record has wall time and peak memory for all five libraries:

  | Library | Caliper | RDT | Speed ratio | Caliper memory | RDT memory |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Mantine | 286 ms | 4.7 s | 16× | 219 MiB | 539 MiB |
  | Chakra | 903 ms | 59 s | 66× | 451 MiB | 2,084 MiB |
  | shadcn/ui | 629 ms | 10.2 s | 16× | 353 MiB | 1,400 MiB |
  | Ant Design | 156 ms | 6.1 s | 39× | 179 MiB | 1,038 MiB |
  | React Spectrum | 274 ms | 6.0 s | 22× | 233 MiB | 816 MiB |

  The median is about 22×. This is on a CI machine, and the October 28× was on a laptop, so the page must not mix them.
- **Honest caveats to carry:** Caliper's time is the median of five runs and the others are single runs. The Storybook first answer on the large gate project is 402 to 562 ms against a 150 ms target, a failed gate in ADR 0026. A "limits before claims" page should say that.
- **Proposed shape, same as the parity page:**
  1. Claim: faster, lighter, and fast in Storybook.
  2. How it was measured.
  3. Per-library time as `ComparisonBars` (scaled per library, since the ratio is the story), then memory.
  4. Storybook request path: the lazy first story, 55–121 ms against 357–425 ms, from the changelog.
  5. Counts table with paired rows.
  6. Limits.

**Main Caliper page**
- **Remaining from the audit:**
  - The 28× card is the October laptop figure, so it should become the current 22× median, with the CI caveat.
  - The "Go deeper" "4 ms" card is October.
  - The "Why Caliper" intro should lead with a finding (2 wrong against 289, 89% to 98% of real components) instead of a generic claim.
  - The page still lacks a "how it works" section, a comparison with react-docgen and RDT, and a real TOON sample for agents.
  - The roadmap should name the checker-as-default step honestly, including the failed first-answer gate.
- **Hero:** the kicker and the `art`/`meta` slot refactor are still waiting on your yes.

**Shared fix:** put the November 9 values in one typed data module with their date and source, and have all three pages read from it. Today they're hard-coded in the parity page and the page data, so the figures can drift.

I'd do it in this order: the shared data module, then the measurement page, then the main page's figures and intro, then "how it works" and the comparison table. Shall I start with the data module and the measurement page?

result: The measurement page is stale and partly wrong (October data, an unsourced figure, a false baseline claim), while the main page has a few leftovers. The November 9 record gives current time and memory for all five libraries, so I recommend a shared data module first, then the measurement page. No changes made.

For parity, each repo is pinned to a commit and installed with its own package manager. We remove tests, stories, demos and declaration files, then give both tools the same source files. Caliper uses full HTML attributes, includes unexported components and loads installed dependencies.

-

We match components by file and name. On shared components we count RDT’s non-React props that Caliper finds; on shared props we compare Storybook control kinds and type text. A separate TypeScript 7.1 checker run tests type structure because RDT is not ground truth. Explore the prop results.

-

The weekly parity run checks these rates against a committed baseline and flags growing loss patterns. When comparing a new build with a base build, the harness interleaves their runs and flags a slowdown over 10% on any library. The baseline’s old timing is a record, not the speed gate.

+  <PageSection id="storybook-heading" label="3 · Storybook" title="What does a story feel like?" description="Storybook asks for one component at a time, so the lazy session matters more than the batch run. On Chakra with dependencies the first story answers in 55 to 121 ms.">
-  <PageSection id="dev-heading" label="03 / dev" title="Save, ask, answer" description="A warm session changes the work. This is the Storybook request path under active development.">

-
1

Save a file

The component source changes while Storybook stays open.

-
2

Check freshness

The session checks saved edits before answering a docgen request.

-
3

Resolve the story

The on-demand path asks for the component the story needs.

-
4

Return prop docs

Storybook gets argTypes, defaults and descriptions.

-

On-demand resolution shipped in the 0.10.0 addon. These source results predate it and are not package benchmarks.
+  <PageSection id="details-heading" label="the counts" title="The numbers behind the bars" description={`Weekly record of ${record.dateLabel}, Caliper ${record.caliper}, on a CI runner.`}>

+    <Table caption="Time and peak memory, Caliper and RDT" groupSize={2} rowTones={libraries.flatMap(() => ['focus' as const, 'reference' as const])} columns={['library', 'tool', 'time', 'peak memory', 'against RDT']} rows={libraries.flatMap((library) => [[library.name, 'Caliper', seconds(library.msC), mib(library.mibC), `${ratio(speedRatio(library))} faster, ${ratio(memoryRatio(library))} less memory`], [library.name, 'RDT', seconds(library.msR), mib(library.mibR), 'baseline']])} />
-  <PageSection id="requests-heading" label="the requests" title="What the addon spent" description="129 real React Spectrum stories, with fallback disabled so every request reaches Caliper.">

-

The biggest win came from replacing a JavaScript directory sweep on every request with one native freshness check per story. Session startup also stopped sending every component’s props to JavaScript just to build an index.

-

These times cover the addon’s request path. They do not include browser rendering, Storybook’s UI work or a full page load. The before and after builds ran interleaved, best of three.
+  <PageSection id="care-heading" label="falls short" title="Where it falls short" description="Fast is not the same as fast enough on every project.">

+
  • First answers on very large projects. A project with 1,616 components answers in 402 to 562 ms against a 150 ms target, so that gate in ADR 0026 failed. The floor today is about 230 ms, and most of the answer is Chakra’s style-prop lists.

+
  • CI timing is noisy. A shared runner moves by 10% or more from week to week, so read the ratios, not the milliseconds.

+
  • The runs differ in count. Caliper’s time is the median of five runs and RDT’s is one run.

+
  • Session memory was measured on macOS arm64 only. The peak was 446 MiB over 650 edits.

+

Prop correctness has its own page, Are the props right?
-  <PageSection id="lazy-heading" label="the engine" title="Pay for what you open" description="A separate Rust session experiment shows why on-demand lookup is promising.">

Chakra session start45 ms

Lazy start, down from 352 ms in batch. Dependencies and full HTML attributes on.

peak after 50 components137 MiB

Lazy peak, down from 532 MiB in batch. The requests used a fixed selection.

-      <figcaption class={small}>Source experiment, October 24. Times run from process start to the last answer. This is the Rust API beneath the binding, not a Storybook page-load measurement. Lazy and batch answers were checked for equivalence.</figcaption>
-  <PageSection id="care-heading" label="caveats" title="What to remember" content="text">

-
  • Version matters. The five-library parity numbers are Caliper 0.4.0 from October 23. Newer releases need the same run again.

-
  • The clocks differ. Cold Node startup is shared; installed-library Caliper time includes process start while RDT time does not; addon request time leaves out browser rendering.

-
  • Project shape matters. A large dependency graph can raise both latency and memory. The pinned repos expose that cost better than fixture files alone.

-
  • TypeScript 7.1 is separate. The checker is a measurement oracle. Caliper’s semantic extraction pass is an experimental CLI opt-in in source, not a Storybook feature yet.

// median of five runs for Caliper, one run for RDT.
export const record = {
  date: '2026-11-09',
  dateLabel: 'November 9, 2026',
  caliper: '0.10.0',
} as const

export interface LibraryRecord {
  name: string
  wrongC: number
  wrongR: number
  /** Props each tool lists in the checker's universe. */
  nC: number
  nR: number
  /** The share of listed props that match the checker. */
  listC: number
  listR: number
  verdict: 'better' | 'close' | 'behind'
  lessC: number
  lessR: number
  /** The share of real components Caliper reports, and the count it is of. */
  comps: number
  compsOf: string
  msC: number
  msR: number
  mibC: number
  mibR: number
}

export const libraries: readonly LibraryRecord[] = [
  {
    name: 'Mantine',

content.text:
The measurement page is rebuilt, and the main page's figures now come from the same dated record as the parity page. The `orin-dx` format, typecheck, lint and test checks all exit 0. I screenshotted the new measurement page in full and the main page's "How it stacks up" section at desktop width in light theme only. I did not re-screenshot after the last deep-dive card tweak, and did not run the site build or `verify`.

**The headline, speed and memory together:** across the five libraries, Caliper is 16× to 66× faster than RDT (median 22×) and uses 2.5× to 5.8× less memory (median 4×). The memory side is called out as prominently as the speed side. For Chakra, RDT takes 59 s and 2,084 MiB; Caliper takes 903 ms and 451 MiB. That is the November 9 weekly record on a CI runner.

**Measurement page flow:** one idea per section, each description bridging to the next.
- **Opening:** the claim, with both ratios.
- **"How we measured":** three short steps.
- **"1 · speed" and "2 · memory":** one chart each, with the ratio on every pair. The speed chart scales each pair on its own, because the ratio is the story.
- **"3 · Storybook":** two charts from the 0.10.0 changelog on Chakra. The lazy session answers its first story in 55 to 121 ms against 357 to 425 ms eager, and uses 419 MB against 658 MB.
- **"The numbers behind the bars":** the paired-row table.
- **"Where it falls short":** four bullets. The large-project first answer is 402 to 562 ms against a 150 ms target, a failed gate in ADR 0026. CI timing is noisy. Caliper's time is a median of five runs and RDT's is one run. Session memory was measured on macOS arm64 only.

I removed the unsourced "0.38 s" chart, the October laptop table, the false "committed baseline" claim and the filler four-step diagram.

**One shared record:** the new `data/caliperRecord.ts` holds the November 9 figures with their date. The parity page, measurement page, main page figures, and the family metrics all read from it. The deep-dive card now shows the per-library range (16–66× and 2.5–5.8×), so it adds something beyond the 22× card above it. The stale roadmap line is replaced with the real open work.

**Still open:**
- **Main page:** the "how it works" section, the comparison with react-docgen and RDT, a real TOON sample, and the "Why" intro leading with a finding.
- **Hero:** the kicker and the `art`/`meta` slot refactor are still waiting on your yes.
- **Dead code:** `ParityPlot` is unused.
- **Caliper-side change for trust:** score RDT on real components and list the props behind each count. Not planned yet.
- **Not committed:** nothing in the pages repo is committed.

---
import Base from './Base.astro'
import ReadingPage from '@pages/components/frame/readingPage.astro'
import { ToolPageHero } from '../components/tool-page-hero/toolPageHero.tsx'
import { tools } from '../data/tools.ts'
import { Breadcrumbs } from '@pages/foundations/ui/breadcrumbs'
import { caliperEvidenceCrumb, caliperEvidenceSwitcher, caliperEvidenceTrail, toolStructuredData, type CaliperEvidenceTopic } from '../data/toolNav.ts'
import { toolBreadcrumbPlacement } from '../components/tool-breadcrumbs/toolBreadcrumbPlacement.ts'

interface Props {
  title: string
  summary: string
  topic: CaliperEvidenceTopic
}
const { title, summary, topic } = Astro.props
const caliper = tools.find((tool) => tool.id === 'caliper')!
---

<Base title={`${title} · Caliper · Orin DX`} description={summary} current="tools" family="build">
  <ReadingPage>
    <Breadcrumbs
      slot="breadcrumbs"
      client:load
      items={caliperEvidenceTrail()}
      current={caliperEvidenceCrumb(topic)}
      switcher={caliperEvidenceSwitcher()}
      structuredData={toolStructuredData}
      classes={{ root: toolBreadcrumbPlacement() }}
    />
    <ToolPageHero tool={caliper} art="none" title={title} description={summary} />
    <slot />
  </ReadingPage>
</Base>

---
import Base from './Base.astro'
import ReadingPage from '@pages/components/frame/readingPage.astro'
import { ToolPageHero } from '../components/tool-page-hero/toolPageHero.tsx'
import { tools } from '../data/tools.ts'
import { Breadcrumbs } from '@pages/foundations/ui/breadcrumbs'
import { caliperEvidenceCrumb, caliperEvidenceSwitcher, caliperEvidenceTrail, toolStructuredData, type CaliperEvidenceTopic } from '../data/toolNav.ts'
import { toolBreadcrumbPlacement } from '../components/tool-breadcrumbs/toolBreadcrumbPlacement.ts'

interface Props {
  title: string
  summary: string
  topic: CaliperEvidenceTopic
}
const { title, summary, topic } = Astro.props
const caliper = tools.find((tool) => tool.id === 'caliper')!
---

<Base title={`${title} · Caliper · Orin DX`} description={summary} current="tools" family="build">
  <ReadingPage>
    <Breadcrumbs
      slot="breadcrumbs"
      client:load
      items={caliperEvidenceTrail()}
      current={caliperEvidenceCrumb(topic)}
      switcher={caliperEvidenceSwitcher()}
      structuredData={toolStructuredData}
      classes={{ root: toolBreadcrumbPlacement() }}
    />
    <ToolPageHero tool={caliper} art="none" title={title} description={summary} />
    <slot />
  </ReadingPage>
</Base>
